candidates.attacker_control: The XML being parsed: DefaultXMLParser reads the parameter type from an XML attribute (XMLConfiguration.DEFAULT_ATT_PARAMETER_TYPE = "t") and calls Class.forName on it (DefaultXMLParser.java:366-369); the parameter element body is attacker-written XML that is then unmarshalled by XStream. In the platform this XML arrives through filter-stream inputs (e.g. import/convert sources such as XAR/filter XML). For the SafeXStream instances the XML comes from job-status/history files, which are normally server-written but are read back with the same unrestricted unmarshaller.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The repository contains no XStream addPermission/allowTypes/setupDefaultSecurity call anywhere (grep for addPermission/allowTypes/setupDefaultSecurity: none); only the commented-out setupDefaultSecurity in SafeXStream. I checked whether the unmarshaller restricts the root class: XMLTreeUnmarshaller.start() uses the type from the DataHolder, which is exactly the attacker/caller-selected class, and nested element names are still resolved by XStream's mapper. Long-standing FIXME/TODO comments show the security bypass is intentional for job serialization, which argues this is an accepted design risk rather than a one-line regression; SafeXStream's SafeReflectionProvider/XStreamUtils only filter *serialization* of unserializable fields, not unmarshalling of attacker types. No in-repo HTTP endpoint reaches the filter parser, so exploitation depends on the platform's import/filter APIs and on required rights.
candidates.impact: Remote code execution in the XWiki server process (arbitrary classes instantiated/deserialized, classic XStream gadget chains), or at minimum arbitrary object instantiation and outbound requests via gadget classes. A deserialization primitive on server-side XML is normally treated as critical/high.
candidates.prerequisites: Ability to make the server parse attacker-supplied filter XML (e.g. import/filter-conversion rights) or to place a crafted status/history XML file. A gadget class available on the classpath and XStream 1.4.17 (pin in the parent pom) not blocking it; the parameter must map to a filter parameter whose declared type allows the type attribute (the serializer writes that attribute for Object-typed parameters).
candidates.root_cause: Untrusted XML is deserialized with XStream without any type allow-list, and XStream's own security mechanism is deliberately bypassed. In the filter-XML parser, the Java type of a parameter is read from the XML itself and loaded with Class.forName, then passed as XStream's root type; the XStream used for parameters (ParameterXStream/NoWarningXStream) overrides unmarshal() to call the marshalling strategy directly, skipping the security warning/checks and registering no permissions. The shared SafeXStream similarly leaves XStream's default security unconfigured (the call is commented out) and overrides unmarshal() the same way, so the root object/element names in the XML control which classes are instantiated.
candidates.title: Unrestricted XStream deserialization of attacker-controlled filter/job XML (arbitrary class selection, no type allow-list)
candidates.trace: 1) DefaultXMLParser.unserializeParameter: element.hasAttribute(configuration.getAttributeParameterType()) -> Class.forName(typeString, true, TCCL) with the attribute value from the untrusted document (lines 364-369); 2) XStreamParameterManager.unSerialize puts the attacker-selected type in the DataHolder and calls xstream.unmarshal(new DomReader(rootElement), null, dataHolder) (lines 110-127); 3) ParameterXStream exposes that XStream with only aliases/converters and no permissions, and NoWarningXStream.unmarshal() calls marshallingStrategy.unmarshal(...) directly, bypassing XStream's security check/warning path (NoWarningXStream.java:62-74, ParameterXStream.java:42-75); 4) the same bypass exists for the shared SafeXStream (initialize() leaves setupDefaultSecurity commented out, unmarshal() bypasses XStream.unmarshal), used by JobStatusSerializer and DefaultExtensionJobHistorySerializer, so any attacker-influenced status/history XML also reaches unrestricted deserialization.
candidates.unverified: I could not run or build anything, cannot confirm a concrete gadget chain for the pinned XStream 1.4.17 in this classpath, and cannot confirm that any XWiki platform import/convert endpoint actually forwards attacker-controlled 't' type attributes for an Object-typed filter parameter (that routing lives outside this repository). It is therefore a lead, not a runtime-confirmed RCE.

coverage_summary: Reviewed the assigned snapshot (1419 model-visible files; main sources only, tests/resources largely stripped; binary-like files skipped by the tools). Inspected or searched: xwiki-commons-xml (HTML cleaner filters, SecureHTMLElementSanitizer and definitions, XMLUtils, DefaultXMLReaderFactory, LocalEntityResolver, StAX/Sax2Dom), xwiki-commons-velocity (engine, configuration, SecureIntrospector/Uberspector, VelocityParser, tools), xwiki-commons-filter and filter-xml (DefaultXMLParser, XStreamParameterManager/ParameterXStream/NoWarningXStream, input/output sources), xwiki-commons-xstream (SafeXStream, Safe* wrappers, XStreamUtils/checkers), xwiki-commons-extension (serializer, repositories incl. HTTP/Aether/XWiki, handlers, job history, PathUtils/ExtensionUtils), xwiki-commons-job (DefaultJobStatusStore/serializer, script service), netflux (endpoint, channels, JSON), script safe wrappers, crypto-password KDFs/encryptor, classloader, websocket, properties, configuration, context, component, environment, and the parent POM dependency versions. Targeted greps for dangerous APIs (exec/ProcessBuilder, ObjectInputStream, XML hardening flags, addPermission/allowTypes, File IO, reflection/Class.forName, setAccessible) and for security-relevant comments were used; no build, tests, or runtime checks were performed.
limitations: No execution/build/test run and no git history or diffs available, so none of the findings is runtime-confirmed and I cannot prove which lines (if any) differ from upstream.
Tests were stripped from the snapshot, removing regression evidence that could point to the intended vulnerable behavior.

Reachability from XWiki platform endpoints (import/filter-conversion/status XML) lives outside this repository and could not be verified; the XStream candidate may require rights that limit attacker control.
Large modules (crypto internals, Aether/XWiki repository clients, Maven/XAR tooling, cache/logging internals) were reviewed only selectively; I did not exhaustively read all 1419 files.
Dependency-level issues (e.g. the pinned XStream 1.4.17 / commons-compress 1.21) were noted but not confirmed against a specific advisory.

rejected_leads.lead: HTML sanitizer bypass (SecureHTMLElementSanitizer / SanitizerFilter / HTMLDefinitions / SVGDefinitions / MathMLDefinitions)
rejected_leads.reason: This is a faithful DOMPurify port (allow-lists, ATTR_WHITESPACE/IS_ALLOWED_URI/IS_NO_URI/IS_SCRIPT_OR_DATA/DATA_ATTR logic all present and fail-closed). I could not construct or verify a concrete mutation/naming bypass from source alone, so it stays a hardening-area suspicion rather than a source-evidenced vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: XXE in DefaultExtensionSerializer.getExtensionElement (default DocumentBuilderFactory parsing extension descriptor InputStreams)
rejected_leads.reason: Real missing hardening (no disallow-doctype-decl, no external-entity disabling) and descriptors can be remote, but exploitation requires attacker control of an extension repository/descriptor and I found no in-repo attacker path; reported as an unconfirmed weaker lead than the deserialization issue.

rejected_leads.lead: XMLUtils.parse(LSInput) sets DISABLE_EXTERNAL_DOCTYPE_DECLARATION to false despite the 'Avoid XXE' comment
rejected_leads.reason: The same block disables external parameter and general entities, so no working XXE is evident; DOCTYPE allowance also looks required by UnifiedHTMLDiffManager, which always feeds a document containing a DOCTYPE. Internal-entity expansion DoS is possible in principle but not confirmed.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultJobStatusStore.encode() does not escape '.' (unlike PathUtils.encode), so job ids containing '..' can traverse out of the status store
rejected_leads.reason: Source-visible asymmetry, but I could not establish that any reachable job id component can be '..' without appropriate rights, and the fixed file name (status.xml[.zip]) limits impact; kept as an unconfirmed lead.

rejected_leads.lead: LocalEntityResolver.resolveEntity returns null for unknown entities ('will try online'), XMLUtils.formatXMLContent XSLT/new transformer usage, VelocityParser missing 'try' in its directive sets
rejected_leads.reason: Long-standing designs or no demonstrated security impact; not tied to attacker-controlled data with concrete impact.

summary: xwiki-commons 14.9-rc-1 (1419 main-source files, tests stripped). The strongest source-evidenced issue is unrestricted XStream deserialization of untrusted XML: the filter-XML parser lets the document name an arbitrary Java class (parameter "type" attribute -> Class.forName) and then hands the element to an XStream instance that explicitly bypasses XStream's security machinery and configures no type permissions; the same no-allow-list pattern exists in the shared SafeXStream used for job status/extension-history XML. Impact if an attacker can get the server to parse crafted filter/status XML (e.g. through a filter-stream/import path) is arbitrary object instantiation and RCE via known XStream gadget chains. No concrete XSS bypass of the HTML sanitizer, no confirmed XXE, and no confirmed path traversal met the evidence bar for a second candidate.
